The laundromat was busiest on rainy Sundays. People arrived carrying damp bags and the private hope that a dryer might fix more than their clothes.

One afternoon, a little boy discovered that the machines made different notes when he tapped them with a plastic spoon. He moved down the row, listening carefully: low, low, high, lower. His mother started to tell him to stop, but an older man near the window began humming along.

Soon the boy was taking requests. He couldn’t play any of them, of course, but he listened to each one seriously before returning to his machines. A woman asked for a song her father used to sing. The boy struck three dryers, paused, and struck one again. “That’s the part where he forgets the words,” he said.

The woman laughed, then looked away for a moment.

By the time the rain stopped, the boy had been paid in two peppermints, a sticker, and a quarter. His mother folded their warm clothes into neat stacks, and he tucked the spoon into his pocket like a musician packing up after a show.
